title: Chapter 3 Quiz
description: Test your mastery of IAM – users, groups, policies, roles, MFA, and best practices.

questions.question: What type of AWS service is IAM?
questions.explanation: IAM is a global service. You don't need to select a region to manage identities.

questions.question: Which entity has unrestricted access to an AWS account by default?
questions.explanation: The root user is created at sign‑up and has full access. IAM users start with no permissions.

questions.question: An IAM user created in the us-east-1 region can only access resources in that region.
questions.explanation: False. IAM users are global and can access any region, provided their policies allow it.

questions.question: What is the maximum number of IAM groups a single user can belong to?
questions.explanation: A user can be a member of up to 10 groups. This is a soft limit that can be increased by request, but 10 is the default.

questions.question: When multiple IAM policies apply to a user, what is the evaluation logic?
options: Only the most restrictive policy counts
Policies are evaluated in alphabetical order
An explicit Deny overrides any Allow; otherwise any Allow grants the permission
The user chooses which policy to use
questions.explanation: AWS evaluates all policies. If any statement explicitly Denies, the request is denied. Otherwise, at least one Allow statement is needed.

questions.question: Which element in an IAM policy statement defines the allowed or denied AWS API actions?
questions.explanation: The Action element lists the API operations (e.g., s3:GetObject). Effect is Allow or Deny.

questions.question: The JSON element that uniquely identifies a resource in AWS is called an ________.
questions.explanation: Amazon Resource Name (ARN) uniquely identifies resources like arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket.

questions.question: You want to grant a user read‑only access to all S3 buckets. Which AWS managed policy should you attach?
questions.explanation: AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess provides read‑only permissions for all S3 resources.

questions.question: What is a key advantage of using customer managed policies over inline policies?
options: They are free, inline policies cost money
They can be reused across multiple users, groups, or roles
Customer managed policies are automatically updated by AWS
questions.explanation: Customer managed policies are standalone objects that you can attach to many identities. Inline policies are embedded and not reusable.

questions.question: An IAM role differs from a user mainly because:
options: Roles provide temporary credentials and don’t have a password or permanent access keys
Roles can only be used in the console
questions.explanation: Roles are meant to be assumed; they issue temporary credentials via STS. Users have long‑term credentials.

questions.question: Which policy defines who can assume an IAM role?
questions.explanation: The trust policy specifies which principals (users, services, accounts) are allowed to call sts:AssumeRole.

questions.question: When you assign an IAM role to an EC2 instance, how does the instance obtain credentials?
options: You must manually copy an access key to the instance
The instance profile automatically makes temporary credentials available via the instance metadata service
The role’s secret key is encrypted in the AMI
questions.explanation: The EC2 instance retrieves temporary security credentials from 169.254.169.254 (metadata), and they are rotated automatically.

questions.question: Which of the following is a virtual MFA option for AWS?
questions.explanation: Virtual MFA applications like Google Authenticator or Authy run on your phone. YubiKey is a hardware MFA (U2F).

questions.question: It is safe to hard‑code AWS access keys in application code if the repository is private.
questions.explanation: False. Never store credentials in source code. They can be leaked, and even private repos can become compromised. Use environment variables or IAM roles.

questions.question: Which tool lets you test IAM policies without affecting real resources?
questions.explanation: The IAM Policy Simulator evaluates policies and reports whether a specific action would be allowed or denied.

questions.question: What does an IAM Credential Report provide?
options: A list of all running EC2 instances
Details about every IAM user’s password age, MFA status, and access key usage
A graph of API calls over time
questions.explanation: The Credential Report is a CSV file that helps you audit IAM user credentials.

questions.question: To allow users from another AWS account to access your resources, you should:
options: Create an IAM user for them in your account
Create a role with a trust policy allowing their account, and let them assume it
questions.explanation: Cross‑account roles are the secure way to grant access to external AWS accounts without sharing credentials.

questions.question: Which AWS service can alert you if an S3 bucket policy allows public access?
questions.explanation: IAM Access Analyzer continuously monitors policies and alerts on resources shared with external entities.

questions.question: What is the 'Principle of Least Privilege'?
options: Give users full access so they aren't blocked
Grant the minimum permissions required to perform a task
Deny all actions by default and never grant permissions
questions.explanation: Least privilege means starting with zero permissions and adding only what is necessary.

questions.question: What does `sts:AssumeRole` API do?
options: Returns temporary security credentials for a role
questions.explanation: STS (Security Token Service) AssumeRole is how you get the temporary keys to act as that role.

questions.question: IAM roles can only be assumed by AWS services, not by IAM users.
questions.explanation: False. IAM users can also assume roles (if the trust policy allows), which is useful for cross‑account access or temporary elevated permissions.

questions.question: Which password policy setting forces users to pick a new password periodically?
options: Require at least one uppercase letter
questions.explanation: Password expiration (e.g., 90 days) requires users to change their password after the set period.

questions.question: Access keys are used for:
questions.explanation: Access keys (ID + secret) are for API, CLI, and SDK authentication, not for the console.

questions.question: What is an instance profile?
options: A profile picture for your EC2 instance
A container for an IAM role that you can attach to an EC2 instance
questions.explanation: An instance profile allows an EC2 instance to assume a role and obtain temporary credentials.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an IAM best practice?
options: Enable MFA for the root account
Use the root account for daily operations
questions.explanation: Using root for daily work is strongly discouraged. Create an IAM admin user instead.
